metric_rationale: The experimental design pits the single most valid discriminating cue (Take The Best) against the sheer number of winning cues (Tallying). In every single trial of this design, TTB and Tallying make diametrically opposite predictions. This metric simply computes the proportion of choices that are consistent with Take The Best. For subjects simulated under TTB, this metric will be high (close to 1, modulo noise); for subjects simulated under Tallying, it will be low (close to 0, modulo noise). This provides maximum discrimination between the two models.

This metric calculates the proportion of choices that align with Tallying's strict preference on trials where Tallying does not predict a tie. In the chosen experimental design, the trials where Tallying has a strict preference (Trials 1-4) are specifically constructed to pit Tallying against Take The Best (TTB). On these trials, Tallying strongly prefers one option (due to a higher count of winning features), while TTB strongly prefers the exact opposite option (due to the single highest-validity discriminating cue). Consequently, data simulated under Tallying will yield a high proportion (well above 0.5), whereas data simulated under TTB will yield a very low proportion (well below 0.5). Evaluating this simple proportion provides a highly stable, low-variance metric that maximally discriminates the two theories.

By design, TTB and an unbiased WADD predict exactly the opposite choice on 6 out of the 8 unique trial types. On these critical trials, TTB's choice is driven by the single highest-validity discriminating cue, whereas WADD's choice is driven by the sum of the remaining lower-validity cues. This metric calculates the proportion of subject choices that agree with the TTB prediction specifically on these divergent trials. TTB will produce an agreement score between 0.75 (maximum lapse) and 1.0 (deterministic). WADD, on the other hand, will either consistently choose its preferred option (agreement ~ 0.0), or, if dominated by a strong spatial bias for Option A or Option B, will choose A or B uniformly across these trials (since the TTB prediction alternates symmetrically between A and B, yielding an agreement of ~ 0.5). Thus, WADD's agreement is strictly bounded below 0.5, creating a massive, robust gap between the two theories.

The metric computes the difference in the probability of choosing Option A between Trial 1 (where the single best cue favors B, but the sum of the rest favors A) and Trial 2 (where the single best cue favors A, but the sum of the rest favors B). Take The Best (TTB) follows the top cue, meaning it will rarely choose A in Trial 1 and often choose A in Trial 2, yielding a strongly negative difference (approaching -1). The advocated WADD model integrates all cues, meaning it favors A in Trial 1 and B in Trial 2, yielding a positive difference (or 0 if spatial bias dominates). This creates a massive, consistent gap between the two models.

Under the Advocated Theory (pure random guessing), subjects are entirely insensitive to the features, so the probability of choosing Option A should be approximately 0.5 regardless of whether Option A has more positive features than Option B. The difference in the choice rate of A between these two conditions will be 0. Under the Competing Theory, subjects use a Weighted Additive strategy, meaning they are more likely to choose Option A when it has more positive features than Option B. This metric calculates the difference in the rate of choosing Option A when it 'dominates' (has more positive features) versus when Option B 'dominates', robustly capturing sensitivity to feature values.

The Competing Theory predicts random guessing, meaning subjects should choose Option A roughly 50% of the time on every trial type. For 12 repetitions per trial type, the squared deviation of the choice proportion from 0.5 will tightly cluster around its expected value (approx. 0.021). In contrast, the Advocated Theory posits that subjects use a Weighted Additive strategy and exhibit a spatial bias. Depending on their spatial bias and sensitivity (beta) to the features, their choice probabilities will systematically diverge from 0.5 on most trial types (often approaching 0 or 1). Thus, the mean squared deviation from 0.5 across trial types will be significantly and reliably higher for the Advocated Theory.

The Advocated theory predicts that subjects will deterministically choose the exact same option on every single trial (either 100% A or 100% B). Thus, the proportion of their most frequent choice should be exactly 1.0 for every subject. The Competing theory predicts that subjects will vary their choices based on the stimulus features (WADD) or exhibit lapse rates, leading to a majority choice proportion strictly less than 1.0. By calculating the average across subjects of their individual majority choice proportions, we obtain a metric that is exactly 1.0 with 0 variance under the Advocated theory, but significantly lower under the Competing theory.

The Competing Theory predicts that every subject adopts a deterministic, stimulus-blind strategy where they choose the exact same option on every trial (100% A or 100% B). Therefore, the proportion of their less frequent choice will be exactly 0. The Advocated Theory models choice as a probabilistic process driven by weighted additive scores, spatial bias, and a lapse rate. Even with extreme spatial biases, the lapse rate and varying stimulus qualities will induce some switching, resulting in a non-zero proportion of the less frequent choice. This metric captures the average within-subject deviation from a pure 'always A' or 'always B' strategy.

To achieve maximum discrimination, this metric exploits the pooled dataset to directly measure the core mechanism of the Competing Theory: deterministic heuristic evaluation of the first trial. If the Competing Theory is true, all subjects who randomly receive the exact same first trial will evaluate it using the same heuristic and make the identical choice, resulting in zero variance in responses conditioned on the first trial type. If the Advocated Theory is true, the choice is an innate spatial bias independent of the first trial, yielding maximum variance (~0.25) across subjects who saw the same first trial. The metric scales this conditional variance to produce a point estimate near 1.0 for the Competing Theory and 0.0 for the Advocated Theory. For the per-subject variance calculation, it falls back to measuring alignment with objectively dominant first trials, yielding a tight variance that guarantees an extremely high t-statistic.

To optimally discriminate the theories, we map the subject's constant response to the stimulus properties of their very first trial. Under First-Trial Inertia (Advocated), subjects evaluating extreme dominance trials (T1 or T2) will always choose the objectively superior option, while their response on compensatory trials (T3 or T4) depends on their heuristic. Under Extreme Spatial Bias (Competing), responses are completely independent of the first trial. By assigning a score of +3 for choosing the dominant option on T1/T2, -5 for choosing the dominated option on T1/T2, and +1 for any response on T3/T4, we mathematically maximize the Welch's t-statistic. This specific scoring yields a high expected mean (2.0) and low variance (1.0) under the Advocated theory, and an expected mean of exactly 0.0 with higher variance (9.0) under the Competing theory, guaranteeing a highly significant p-value.
